title: CLIP & Contrastive Image–Text Alignment
interviewAnswer: CLIP trains an image encoder and text encoder so matched image-caption pairs have high cosine similarity and mismatched pairs have lower similarity. A contrastive loss over a batch creates a shared embedding space, which enables zero-shot classification and cross-modal retrieval.
why: CLIP-style alignment is foundational for retrieval, VLMs and conditioning in modern generative vision systems.
intuition: Put an image and its caption close together on a semantic map while pushing unrelated captions away.
deepDive: Image and text encoders produce vectors that are L2-normalized. Their pairwise dot products form a batch similarity matrix. A learned temperature/logit scale controls sharpness, and symmetric cross-entropy trains both image-to-text and text-to-image matching. At inference, arbitrary class descriptions can become text prototypes for zero-shot prediction.
workedExample: For a batch of three matched image-caption pairs, the desired similarity matrix has its largest values on the diagonal.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that zero-shot classification depends strongly on prompt/class text design and distribution shift.
production: For retrieval, evaluate recall@K across slices and monitor embedding drift when encoders, prompts or preprocessing change.

lab.goal: Build the core CLIP contrastive similarity matrix and verify matched pairs score highest.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
def norm(x): return x/np.linalg.norm(x,axis=1,keepdims=True)
img=norm(np.array([[1.,0.],[0.,1.],[1.,1.]]))
txt=norm(np.array([[.9,.1],[.1,.9],[1.,.8]]))
tau=.1
logits=img@txt.T/tau
print(logits)

visual.caption: CLIP pulls matched image/text embeddings together and pushes mismatched pairs apart with a contrastive objective.
